examGuide.title: Mental model and derivation
examGuide.body:
Microprogrammed control stores control words in a control memory. Horizontal words expose many control signals directly and can be wide; vertical formats encode fields and require decoding. A microsequencer selects the next microinstruction through increments, branches or dispatch. Control-store capacity is word count times word width. A microinstruction is an implementation step, not necessarily a full machine instruction.

**Key relationship:** Control-store capacity = number of microinstructions × microinstruction width

examGuide.title: A repeatable solving procedure
examGuide.body:
1. Separate machine instructions from microinstructions.
2. Count control-store words and word width.
3. Trace sequencing and encoded-field decoding.

examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: A control store maps microinstruction addresses to control signals and next-address decisions. Horizontal encoding exposes many independent control bits; vertical encoding uses compact fields and decoding. Distinguish control-memory word width from address width. Branch conditions and instruction dispatch can make the microprogram nonsequential.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
A control store has 512 microinstructions of 40 bits each. What is its capacity in bytes?

**Answer: 2560.** Capacity is 512·40=20480 bits, or 20480/8=2560 bytes. The microaddress requires 9 bits but is not multiplied into the control-word capacity unless explicitly stored as part of each word.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
Microprogrammed control is not the same as user-program instructions in main memory. Writable control stores and ROM-based stores have different update possibilities.

A microinstruction is not the same as a programmer-visible machine instruction.

examGuide.title: Worked question patterns
examGuide.body:
#### Pattern 1 · MCQ

A control store with 256 words of 40 bits has capacity:

- **A.** 256 bits
- **B.** 1024 bits
- **C.** 10240 bits
- **D.** 102400 bits

**Answer: C.** Multiply word count by width: 256·40=10240 bits.

#### Pattern 2 · MSQ

Choose true statements.

- **A.** Horizontal microcode can directly expose control bits
- **B.** Vertical encoding can reduce word width
- **C.** A microinstruction must equal one full ISA instruction
- **D.** Microsequencing can branch on conditions

**Answer: A, B, D.** A/B describe encoding tradeoffs. A machine instruction may need several microinstructions; next-address logic can branch.

#### Pattern 3 · NAT

Address bits needed to select one of 1024 microinstructions?



**Answer: 10.** 2¹⁰=1024, so ten bits select the control-store word.
